summary: Devil's tongue weed is a red seaweed with flat, thick, slippery blades that range from small leaves to blades up to 3 meters long, pink to deep red-brown, with no midrib. It grows in the low tide zone and shallow water, attached to rocks and man-made surfaces. Research from Long Island Sound suggests it may out-compete native seaweeds such as Irish moss and reduce the variety and number of small invertebrates, though its effects appear to be local.
history: Devil's tongue weed is native to the Northwest Pacific. It was first seen on the East Coast in 1994 in Narragansett Bay, Rhode Island, probably brought in ships' ballast water or on ship hulls. It was first found in New York in 2001 at Montauk Point, and its impacts here are still unknown.

handling.text: Do not release it alive. DEC asks people to take several photos from different angles, dispose of the specimen, and report it. Clean, drain and dry boats and equipment before visiting another waterbody, and never dump aquarium contents into waterbodies, ditches or sewers.

report:
New York's official database for invasive species sightings is iMapInvasives, run by the New York Natural Heritage Program (a partnership between SUNY ESF and the NYS Department of Environmental Conservation). You can make a free account and report directly to the online database, which is the preferred method, or use the iMapInvasives mobile app for iPhone and Android, which can upload your records once you have a connection again. If you don't want an account, the site has a public report form; those reports are reviewed by Natural Heritage Program staff each week before being added.

In New York City parks, report what you find instead of removing it yourself. NYC Parks rules forbid cutting, killing or removing any plants, flowers, shrubs or other vegetation without permission from the Parks Commissioner, and forbid chasing, harassing, harming or removing any animal, nest, or the eggs of any amphibian, reptile or bird (56 RCNY §1-04).
